newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: New Zealand expects new world trade round in 1999.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand expects new world trade round in 1999.

text.p: New Zealand predicts a new round of world trade talks will begin in 1999 and expects as the then-chair of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum to play a pivotal role, foreign ministry officials said on Friday.
Richard Nottage, Secretary of Foreign Affairs and Trade, told a briefing of journalists that he expected a new round of talks to further free up global trade in the 21st century.
"New Zealand will be placed to play a pivotal role. The chair of APEC... puts us in a very unique place," Nottage said.
The previous talks, known as the Uruguay Round, stretched over seven years up until 1993 but had far-reaching implications in liberalising trade, particularly in agriculture.
A new cycle of talks over farm products and services is due to begin in 1999 but New Zealand wants, and believes, it will develop into a full, wide-ranging round.

Peter Kennedy, director of the department's Economic Division, said there had been growing acceptance since the inaugural ministerial World Trade Organisation conference in Singapore in December that there would have to be a new round.

"The timing is such that that could evolve into a new multilateral round. There is almost an inevitability given that there are going to be major negotiations in agriculture, services, intellectual property and so on.

"That is not a view shared by everybody. The United States quite likes doing sectorial negotiations and they can point to some recent successes in telecommunications and information technology," he said.
Kennedy said New Zealand's experience was that it was more difficult to achieve success in narrow sectoral talks rather than holding broad, multilateral negotiations.
Agriculture exporting nations such as New Zealand see advantages in extending freer trade in agricultural products were issues such as export subsidies have not been fully settled.
A new trade round would seek to get new commitments on free trade from the 130 WTO member states and bind those countries to them, Kennedy said.
He said agriculture would feature in a new round, as would a move to free up international skies for aviation, while some countries want to tighten rules on intellectual property.
